summary_html: A child dies or suffers serious harm while **under agency supervision**, constituting systemic failure. Federal law mandates disclosure and review to identify causes and reforms.
authority_html:
- **Protect Our Kids Act (PL 112-275)** — federal commission and review requirements  
- **CAPTA §5106a(b)(2)(A)(x)** — mandates public disclosure of child-fatality cases

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
key_cases.holding: Rhode Island DCYF social workers were entitled to qualified immunity on substantive due process claims by twins abused in foster care because the evidence did not show conscience-shocking conduct, and Rhode Island sovereign and qualified immunity barred the state negligence claims.
key_cases.relevance: J.R. v. Gloria is the controlling Rhode Island authority on § 1983 claims for harm suffered under agency supervision, and it also confirms state sovereign and qualified immunity defenses.
key_cases.quote: state officials must have been at least aware of known or likely injuries or abuse and have chosen to ignore the danger to the child

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative duty on a child protection agency to protect a child from private violence, so the county's failure to remove Joshua DeShaney from his abusive father was not a constitutional deprivation.
key_cases.relevance: A First Circuit failure-to-protect claim against DCYF must fit the custody-based 'special relationship' exception DeShaney left open; outside custody there is no federal duty to protect.
key_cases.quote: But nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
key_cases.holding: Dismissal of the section 1983 claims arising from the murder of a teenage state witness in Providence was affirmed because the state's unkept promises of protection did not deprive her of liberty, so neither the special-relationship nor the state-created-danger theory removed the case from DeShaney.
key_cases.relevance: Rivera is the First Circuit's Rhode Island authority on the affirmative-duty exceptions to DeShaney, and it is the case J.R. v. Gloria builds on when it asks whether DCYF's relationship with a child creates a constitutional duty to protect.
key_cases.quote: Merely alleging state actions which render the individual more vulnerable to harm, under a theory of state created danger, cannot be used as an end run around DeShaney's core holding.
